## Abstract
Transport planners use regression coefficients and prediction scores from national travel surveys to judge how much ride-hailing, public transport or electric vehicles change travel. These numbers depend on choices that papers rarely state in full: which records were kept, whether the survey weights were used, how the uncertainty was computed, and how a prediction model was tested. We propose a reproducibility ladder with four rungs (rebuild the sample, rebuild the descriptive tables, refit the published model, refit it under the survey's own sampling design) and apply it to {{ladder.n_studies:r}} published studies of the United States National Household Travel Survey (NHTS); the public files allowed the models of {{ladder.n_l2_attempted:r}} studies to be refitted. The samples of {{ladder.n_sufficient:r}} studies were rebuilt well, and {{ladder.share_l1_exact_close:p0}} per cent of {{ladder.n_l1_graded:i}} printed descriptive values were matched. Where the weighted and the unweighted fit reproduce different numbers, the estimator the paper declared reproduced its printed values: in one study weighted odds ratios matched {{cases.quinn_weighted_share:p0}} per cent of the printed values and unweighted ones {{cases.quinn_naive_share:p0}} per cent. With the replicate weights shipped with the survey, standard errors were a median of {{summary.median_se_ratio:1}} times those of an unweighted fit. This cost came almost entirely from the unequal weights ({{summary.median_r_weights:1}} times); clustering of persons within households ({{summary.median_r_cluster:2}} times) and the replicate formula ({{summary.median_r_formula:2}} times) added little on average, and the standard errors of an unweighted analysis were understated by only {{summary.median_r_unw_cl:2}} times. Under each study's declared inference, {{summary.h3_share:p0}} per cent of the significant coefficients (exact interval {{summary.h3_ci_lo:p0}} to {{summary.h3_ci_hi:p0}} per cent) were not significant under the design, and {{summary.share_sign_flip:p0}} per cent of the coefficients changed sign between the unweighted and the weighted fit. For classification models, oversampling the rarer class before splitting the data raised the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, a score of chance level at fifty per cent and perfection at one hundred per cent, of a random forest from {{ml.afv.grouped.rf:p0}} per cent to {{ml.afv.leaky.rf:p0}} per cent; the printed value was reproduced by neither pipeline. A published regression score, the share of variance explained, of {{p21.w2017.gbm.pub:p0}} per cent was not reproduced ({{p21.w2017.gbm.random:p0}} per cent on held-out households). The machinery is released as two modules of the open-source Python package pynhts.

**Keywords:** National Household Travel Survey; reproducibility; survey weights; replicate-weight variance; data leakage; negative binomial regression

## Introduction

The US National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) is the main public source on how Americans travel. Its waves of 2001, 2009, 2017 and 2022 hold between about eight thousand (2022) and one hundred and fifty thousand households each, with every member's trips on one assigned day, the vehicles, and a long list of household and person attributes. Researchers use the files to estimate who rides, who pays and who emits, and the resulting regression coefficients, odds ratios and prediction scores are read by planners as evidence on ride-hailing, bike-sharing, transit, electric vehicles and vehicle miles travelled [@conway2018; @wu2021; @alberini2021]. A coefficient such as "one more ride-hailing trip per month is associated with more trips per day" is a short sentence that rests on a long chain of decisions: which respondents entered the analysis, whether the survey weights were applied, how the standard error was formed, and, for a prediction model, how it was tested on data it had not seen.

Those decisions matter because the NHTS is not a simple random sample. Households are drawn in strata, persons are clustered within households, response differs by group, and the files therefore carry person and household weights and, for the 2001, 2009 and 2017 waves, between ninety-eight and one hundred replicate weights per record, so that analysts can obtain variance estimates that respect the design [@rust1996; @wolter2007]. Whether to weight a regression is a long-standing question in survey statistics: weights can remove bias when selection depends on the outcome, but they cost efficiency when they do not [@winship1994; @solon2015; @gelman2007; @bollen2016]. Whether to use the design when computing standard errors is less debatable: ignoring clustering and stratification understates uncertainty [@lumley2004]. Demonstrations from health surveys show that an association that is significant in an unweighted analysis can cease to be so once weights and design are respected [@birrell2019; @gard2023]. Regression on NHTS data is routine: the official FHWA/ORNL Compendium of Uses of the NHTS lists {{compendium.n_unique:i}} distinct publications from 2006 to 2025, and the abstracts of {{compendium.mod_n:i}} of them describe a regression or machine-learning analysis ({{compendium.modn_n:i}} of these name the NHTS in the abstract; keyword rules, supplementary material). How often the choices above change the conclusions of such analyses has not been measured.

A second doubt concerns reproducibility more broadly. Computational results are often hard to regenerate from the published description [@peng2011; @stodden2018; @hardwicke2021], and when independent analysts receive the same data and question, defensible but different choices can lead to different conclusions, sometimes in opposite directions [@steegen2016; @silberzahn2018; @schweinsberg2021; @simonsohn2020]. Prediction models add a further layer. Machine learning has entered travel-behaviour research with claims that flexible models beat classical ones [@hagenauer2017; @martinbaos2023; @wang2024benchmark], while the wider literature documents how leakage between training and test data produces over-optimistic scores in many fields [@kapoor2023; @kapoor2024reforms; @rosenblatt2024]. Two leaks are especially relevant here. Creating synthetic examples of a rare class before the data are split puts copies of test rows into training, which inflates scores sharply [@chawla2002; @blagus2013; @demircioglu2024]. Splitting rows at random when rows share a household, a place or a person puts near-duplicates on both sides of the split, and validation designs that respect such structure give lower and more honest scores [@roberts2017; @ploton2020; @vabalas2019]. NHTS rows are exactly of this kind: persons of one household share almost everything that matters.

Work on the NHTS itself has mostly examined the quality of its data, for example selection bias among respondents who agree to follow-up surveys [@wang2022nhts], or used it to answer substantive questions [@conway2018]. Open pipelines exist for synthetic travel demand from other national surveys [@horl2021]. In searches of OpenAlex and Crossref, a duplication test, a ScienceDirect LeapSpace review and a keyword audit of the official Compendium (all described in the supplementary material) we found no study that takes a body of published NHTS analyses, rebuilds their samples and tables, refits their models, and asks whether their conclusions survive the survey's own design and a leakage-free validation. The related work that follows gives the evidence behind this statement. This is a gap in a double sense: the size of the effect of ignoring the design in transport regressions is unknown, and the extent to which published prediction scores depend on the validation pipeline is unknown.

This paper fills the gap with a method and a case study. The method is a reproducibility ladder with four rungs, each of which can be graded against printed numbers, together with a design-aware re-estimation that compares three ways of fitting the same model and a re-scoring of classifiers under four pipelines. The case study applies it to {{ladder.n_studies:r}} published studies of the NHTS, collected as a convenience set, of which {{ladder.n_l2_attempted:r}} could be refitted from the public files. We ask four questions: how much of each study can be rebuilt; whether the printed estimates are reproduced by the estimator the paper declares; how much the conclusions change under the survey design; and how much a prediction score depends on the pipeline. The same machinery is released as two modules of the open-source package pynhts, so that the check takes a few lines of code instead of a few weeks.

## Related work

### Survey design, weights and variance in NHTS research

The NHTS is one of a family of national travel surveys whose designs differ between countries and change between waves [@porschen2026; @svaboe2024; @mcguckin2021]. Within the NHTS series the 2001 wave drew households from a telephone frame and the 2017 wave from an address-based frame; the public files of the 2001, 2009 and 2017 waves carry replicate weights, whereas those of the 2022 wave give strata and clusters for linearisation. Persons, vehicles and trips are tables nested in households, so that any analysis of a person or a trip is an analysis of clustered records with unequal weights.

National descriptive portraits of urban, rural, older-adult and rear-seat travel routinely apply the final weights [@pucher2005; @collia2003; @trowbridge2009; @krumm2012; @wang2023]. Weights improve representation but do not cure missing coverage: work on how well household travel surveys capture vulnerable travellers, people with disabilities, respondents who report no travel at all, and groups that follow-up surveys lose shows that the people and trips that the weights must stand in for are the hardest to observe [@christensen2025; @esekhaigbe2026; @zhang2026; @wang2022nhts; @shaw2021]. Weighting is therefore necessary for a national statement and not sufficient for a correct one.

When the analysis moves from description to regression or choice modelling, the treatment of the design is less visible. Survey-weighted choice models of ride-sourcing [@zou2021] are an exception; regressions of bicycling, immigrant travel, older-adult travel and online shopping on the NHTS [@tribby2019; @porter2020; @barajas2021; @yang2025; @kim2021; @tumula2026] are common, and of the eight regression studies of our own register that we could re-estimate only one used the replicate weights for its variance (@tbl-census). To see how visible the design is in print, we tagged the abstracts of the official FHWA/ORNL Compendium of Uses of the NHTS, whose twelve printed editions and interactive-search export from 2006 to 2025 hold {{compendium.n_records:i}} entries, {{compendium.n_unique:i}} of them distinct. Of the {{compendium.mod_n:i}} abstracts that describe a regression or machine-learning analysis, {{compendium.mod_weights_n:i}} ({{compendium.mod_weights_share:p1}} per cent) name survey weights and {{compendium.mod_variance_n:i}} ({{compendium.mod_variance_share:p1}} per cent) a design-based variance estimator, so that weights are named {{compendium.weights_to_variance_ratio:1}} times as often as variance estimators, and {{compendium.mod_neither_share:p0}} per cent name neither. Among the {{compendium.modn_n:i}} that name the NHTS in the abstract the counts are {{compendium.modn_weights_n:i}} and {{compendium.modn_variance_n:i}}. A reading of every positive found {{compendium.review_weights_tp_n:r}} of {{compendium.review_weights_n:r}} weight flags and {{compendium.review_variance_tp_n:r}} of {{compendium.review_variance_n:r}} variance flags to concern the survey itself. Abstracts are a poor guide to what an analysis did, so these counts show how rarely the design is named, not how rarely it was used; this is the reason for rebuilding the analyses. Design-aware work is concentrated in small-area estimation, where the design is the object of the paper [@vaish2010], and in the few weighted choice models.

The statistical background is old. The variance of an estimate under a complex design is obtained by Taylor linearisation [@woodruff1971] or by replication [@rust1996; @wolter2007], the efficiency of the options and the cost of ignoring the design have been studied for decades [@cohen1986; @johnson1998; @korn1999], and software for it exists in R [@lumley2004] and in commercial packages, whose differences and misuse are also documented [@desousa2000; @brogan2006; @bergtold2018; @richardson2019]. To our knowledge the Python scientific stack has no ready implementation of replicate-weight variance for count models, which is why the engine used in this paper is released in pynhts.

### Reproducibility, analytic flexibility and validation leakage

Beyond the survey, the wider computational sciences have documented how often published results cannot be regenerated from the published description [@peng2011; @stodden2018; @hardwicke2021], and how the conclusions of independent analysts of one data set depend on defensible analytic choices [@silberzahn2018; @schweinsberg2021; @steegen2016; @simonsohn2020]. Travel research is exposed to the same dispersion: a comparison between national surveys, or between survey modes, rests on processing decisions that are seldom reported [@svaboe2024; @nishikawa2022; @verreault2018].

Prediction models add a layer of their own. Benchmarks of machine learning against discrete-choice models, and machine-learning trip models fitted to the NHTS, report that flexible models can match or beat classical ones [@hagenauer2017; @martinbaos2023; @wang2024benchmark; @qawasmeh2024], while audits in other fields trace many over-optimistic scores to leakage between training and test data [@kapoor2023; @kapoor2024reforms; @rosenblatt2024]. Two leaks are known in detail: oversampling a rare class before the split [@chawla2002; @blagus2013; @demircioglu2024] and a random split of rows that share a group [@roberts2017; @ploton2020; @vabalas2019]. Both are plausible in household travel data, in which a rare outcome such as electric vehicle ownership is common material for oversampling and household members are rows with almost the same inputs. In the Compendium, {{compendium.ml_n:i}} abstracts describe machine-learning studies, {{compendium.ml_since_2023_n:i}} of them in the editions of 2023 to 2025; {{compendium.ml_resampling_n:r}} mention oversampling, SMOTE or class imbalance, and {{compendium.ml_accuracy_ge90_n:r}} state an accuracy or area under the curve of at least ninety per cent.

### Gap and contribution

Three questions are therefore open for the NHTS. How large is the effect of ignoring weights and design on published regressions? Which layer of the design produces it: the unequal weights, the clustering in households, or the replicate formula? And how much do published prediction scores depend on the validation pipeline? We found no study that answers them by rebuilding a body of published NHTS analyses. The contribution of this paper is a graded method for doing so, a decomposition of the standard-error difference into its layers, a leakage-free re-scoring of classifiers, and the tools for all three.

## Materials and methods

### The case-study set and the data

The set consists of {{ladder.n_studies:r}} studies published between 2011 and 2025 that analyse the NHTS and print enough numbers to compare with (@tbl-studies). They are listed in the table [@yang2011; @zhou2014; @quinn2016; @deka2019; @jia2019; @krizek2019; @fu2020; @lidbe2021; @alberini2021; @xue2021; @zhang2018bike; @zhang2018veh; @zhang2018ride; @sabouri2020; @jia2020; @jiao2020; @sadeghvaziri2020; @shirgaokar2021; @barua2021; @wu2021; @su2021; @naseralavi2025] and were collected by the authors while building the pynhts package, so they are a convenience set and not a systematic sample of the literature; we draw no conclusion about the share of all NHTS papers that behave like them. Looked up by title in the official NHTS Compendium of Uses, {{compendium.n_case_in_compendium:r}} of the {{ladder.n_studies:r}} are listed, in {{compendium.n_case_domains:r}} of its planning chapters (@tbl-compendium-map); those chapters hold {{compendium.cs_domains_share_of_studies:p0}} per cent of the Compendium's studies, and the {{compendium.n_case_not_in_compendium:r}} studies that are not listed show that the Compendium is itself an incomplete guide. One study was written by the two of us with colleagues, and the first author is also the developer of the package; it is included in the register but was not re-estimated here, so as to avoid grading our own work, and its models are reserved for a separate paper. Public-use NHTS files of 2001, 2009 and 2017 were obtained from the survey's website through pynhts, which verifies each file against its codebook. All {{ladder.n_studies:r}} studies use the 2001, 2009 or 2017 wave.

{{tbl:studies}}

{{tbl:compendium_map}}

### The reproducibility ladder

The ladder has four rungs (@fig-flow). **L0**: rebuild the analysis sample from the public files by applying the paper's rules in the order given, and compare the sample size with the printed one. **L1**: rebuild the descriptive tables and grade every printed value as EXACT (equal at the printed precision), CLOSE (within two per cent), ACCEPTABLE (within five per cent) or GAP. **L2**: fit the published model with the same variables and the estimator the paper declares (weighted or unweighted), and grade each printed coefficient or score in the same way, with a tolerance of at least the last printed digit. **L3**: refit the model under the survey design. No rule was altered to reach a printed number: a difference is recorded as a gap, and the most natural reading of an unwritten rule is documented with the evidence that supported it. Rungs L0 and L1 were completed before this paper's models were run, and their grading is reproduced from the audit files of the package repository. The analysis plan was frozen after three studies (Yang, Quinn, Jiao) had been run during the development of the engine, and these hold about half of the coefficients and all three headline examples; deviations from the plan, including a reformulated fourth hypothesis, are logged in it and summarised in the supplement.

![Method of the paper. Rungs L0 to L3 are applied to each published study; the box V rescoring a classifier applies to machine-learning studies. Diamonds are decisions; dashed boxes record what is carried forward.](figures/fig_flow_en.png){#fig-flow}

### Four ways to fit the same model

Each regression was fitted four ways. The unweighted fit uses maximum likelihood with model-based standard errors, which is what most of the studies report. The clustered fit keeps the unweighted estimate and forms the variance with a sandwich in which observations of the same household form one cluster. The weighted fit uses the person, household or person-day weight of the observation (scaled to the sample size for estimation) with the same household-clustered sandwich; the same fit with every observation its own cluster measures what the unequal weights alone cost. The design-aware fit uses the same weighted estimate with the variance design of the wave. The fits answer different questions: the unweighted estimate describes the association among respondents and the weighted one the association in the population the weights represent, so a comparison of their standard errors mixes a change of estimand with a change of precision; we therefore report the standard errors as a chain of ratios (weights, clustering, replicate formula) and not only their product. For the waves with replicate weights this is the jackknife: the model is refitted with each of the $R$ replicate weights $w_r$, and the variance of a coefficient $\hat\beta$ is
$$\widehat{V}(\hat\beta)=f\sum_{r=1}^{R}\left(\hat\beta_r-\hat\beta\right)^2,$$
with $R=$ {{design.jk_2017:r}} and $f=6/7$ for 2017, $R=$ {{design.jk_2009:r}} and $f=99/100$ for 2009, and $R=$ {{design.jk_2001:r}} and $f=98/99$ for 2001, as in the User's Guides. Logistic, linear and Poisson regressions are refitted exactly from warm starts. Negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial regressions, whose refitting takes minutes, use Newton steps from the full-sample optimum, a step that we checked against exact refits. The count-model likelihoods and their gradients are our own, checked against finite differences and against the statsmodels library [@lambert1992; @zeileis2008]. As independent checks, the logistic, Poisson and linear fits on adults of the 2017 person file were compared with the survey package in R (a replicate-weight design with the same factor): coefficients agreed to one part in one hundred thousand and standard errors to {{design.golden_se_pct:1}} per cent; the Taylor-series variance of the 2022 wave was checked against the same package in the same way. On the weekend negative binomial model of one study, {{design.jk_2017:r}} exact refits gave standard errors within {{newton.max_rel_se_diff:p1}} per cent of the Newton ones. The regime in which a study's printed numbers were reproduced is reported as its declared estimator.

### Models of the case studies

Eight published regression studies were refitted: logistic regression of walking and cycling (two studies); ordinary least squares with fixed effects for vehicle make, state and density (one); negative binomial regression of daily trips (two); and zero-inflated negative binomial regression of monthly shared-mobility use (three). A structural equation model with two latent propensities, a propensity-score matching of ride-hailing user groups, a gradient-boosting regression of household online shopping and five classifiers of alternative-fuel and electric vehicle adoption complete the set. Where a printed coefficient table exists, each printed coefficient is a target of L2; where only a headline is printed (the public-transit effect in two ZINB studies, the elasticity in the OLS study), that headline is the target, and where it was derived from a percentage in the abstract this is stated in the supplement.

### Machine-learning models, validation designs and tuning

Five classifiers were re-run on the sample of {{holdout.n:i}} new-vehicle owners in {{holdout.households:i}} households, with the outcome alternative-fuel vehicle (AFV, {{ml.afv_pos:i}} owners) or electric vehicle (EV, {{ml.ev_pos:i}} owners). The sample rule (newest vehicle of each main driver, at most two model years old, complete key variables) was recovered from the printed sample size and is slightly smaller than the printed one. The models are explained in @tbl-search. Logistic regression turns a weighted sum of the inputs into a probability; the naive Bayes classifier assumes each input to be bell-shaped within a class and independent of the others; a decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions on the inputs; a random forest averages the votes of many trees grown on random parts of the data; and a support vector machine with a radial kernel separates the classes with a smooth boundary built from the training points nearest to it. A sixth family, gradient boosting, which adds small trees one after another so that each corrects the errors of the sum of the earlier ones, was used for the household-level online-shopping regression together with linear regression, a support vector regression and a random forest. These four regression models were not tuned: they were run with fixed, documented settings, those printed in the study where it printed them (cost ten and kernel width one hundredth for the support vector regression, a minimum leaf of twenty-five rows for the forest), because the question was whether the printed scores can be approached with the printed settings.

{{tbl:search}}

Every model was tuned alike. The search space of every model is given in @tbl-search. The search method is random search with the same budget (ten trials) for every model; each trial is scored by three-fold validation inside the training rows, grouped by household in the pipelines that split by household and by row in those that split by row, with oversampling inside the inner training folds only when the pipeline oversamples after the split; the criterion is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. The selected configuration is refitted on all training rows and scored once on the held-out rows (nested validation). The experiment was run with two master seeds. The four pipelines differ only in where the oversampling happens and in what is split. In *oversample, then split rows* the rarer class is oversampled on the whole file by interpolating between near neighbours [@chawla2002], and the rows are then split at random; in *split rows, then oversample* the split comes first and only the training rows are oversampled; in *split households, then oversample* every household lies wholly on one side; and in *split households, no oversampling* the training rows are used as they are and the held-out score is weighted by the survey weight. About {{holdout.afv.n_test:i}} rows, from about {{holdout.households:i}} households, are held out in every split of the household designs (@tbl-holdout), and the frequency histogram of the rare class in all, training and held-out rows is in @fig-holdout of the supplementary material. Because the held-out households are a random subset of all households, the designs test generalisation to new households within the same sample; no held-out group lies outside the range of the training groups, so none is an extrapolation in the sense of a convex hull. For the regression study, a second design holds out whole states, which is a harder test of transfer.

### Software and reproducibility

All numbers, tables and figures are generated by code from the result files; the text contains no typed result. The analysis code, the engine of the regression regimes and the validation pipelines are in the repository, run by one command, and the regression and validation machinery is part of pynhts (modules `pynhts.models` and `pynhts.validate`), with unit tests, a real-data test against R and documentation. The analysis plan, with the hypotheses and thresholds, was written before the models of the second half of the studies were run and is dated.

## Results

### What could be rebuilt

The ladder is shown in @fig-ladder. Of the {{ladder.n_studies:r}} studies, the audit judged the public files sufficient to rebuild the data of {{ladder.n_sufficient:r}}, partly sufficient for {{ladder.n_partial:r}}, and insufficient for {{ladder.n_insufficient:r}}, for which the population or sampling rule is not stated. Over all studies, {{ladder.n_l1_exact:i}} of {{ladder.n_l1_graded:i}} printed descriptive values were reproduced exactly at the printed precision, and {{ladder.share_l1_exact_close:p0}} per cent exactly or within two per cent. The gaps came mostly from the papers: unstated rules for dropping records, arithmetic that does not add up inside a table, and variables that are not in the public file. {{ladder.n_l2_attempted:r}} studies could be taken to the model rung; for the others the reasons are listed in @tbl-studies.

![The ladder for the {{ladder.n_studies:r}} studies. Each row is a study, each column a rung; colours give the grade. The L3 column shows which models were re-estimated, not a grade.](figures/fig_ladder.png){#fig-ladder}

### The declared estimator reproduces the printed numbers

Among the studies in which the unweighted and the weighted fit reproduce clearly different numbers of printed values, the declared estimator reproduced more. The study of walking and cycling by Quinn and colleagues states that population weights and the jackknife were used: the weighted odds ratios matched {{cases.quinn_weighted_ok:r}} of {{cases.quinn_n:r}} printed values and the unweighted ones {{cases.quinn_naive_ok:r}}; for the two commuting models, {{cases.quinn_commute_ok:r}} of {{cases.quinn_commute_n:r}} matched to the printed precision or within two per cent, but for the two transport models few did, which we attribute to the sample (we could not rebuild the printed one). In the study of physical activity by season the weighted odds ratios matched {{cases.yang_weighted_ok:r}} of {{cases.yang_n:r}} printed values and the unweighted ones {{cases.yang_naive_ok:r}}. In the other direction, the negative binomial study of shared mobility and trips, which reports an unweighted fit in R, was reproduced by the unweighted fit ({{cases.jiao_naive_ok:r}} of {{cases.jiao_n:r}} coefficients within two per cent, {{cases.jiao_naive_exact:r}} at the printed precision), and the zero-inflated study of vehicle ownership and ridesharing for {{cases.zhang_naive_ok:r}} of {{cases.zhang_n:r}} coefficients within two per cent and {{cases.zhang_naive_acc:r}} within five per cent. In the other studies neither fit reproduced much: the elasticity of annual miles with respect to fuel cost per mile matched for one of {{cases.alberini_n:r}} printed values ({{cases.alberini_a_ann.naive:3}} against {{cases.alberini_a_ann.pub:3}}). The first hypothesis is therefore supported for the four studies in which the two estimators can be told apart, and not tested for the others; we do not generalise it to all studies.

The estimator matters for the substance, not only for the match. The most striking case is the education effect on cycling to work. The printed odds ratio for a graduate degree compared with the lowest education group is {{cases.quinn_edu_gr.pub:2}}, the weighted fit gives {{cases.quinn_edu_gr.weighted:2}}, and the unweighted fit gives {{cases.quinn_edu_gr.naive:2}}: the sign of the association with education reverses (@fig-weights, reference letter H). The same happens for the Midwest effect on active travel in 2001, with printed {{cases.yang_midwest.pub:2}}, weighted {{cases.yang_midwest.weighted:2}} and unweighted {{cases.yang_midwest.naive:2}}. An unweighted fit estimates the association among respondents, and these results show that respondents differ from the population in ways that matter for this association; we did not test formally whether the weights are informative.

![Odds ratios of cycling to work in the study of Quinn and colleagues: printed, our unweighted fit and our weighted fit with replicate-weight variance. The shaded rows (reference letter H) are the education effects discussed in the text.](figures/fig_weights.png){#fig-weights}

### Standard errors and significance

Across the {{summary.n_coef:r}} re-estimated coefficients of eight regression studies, the design-aware standard error was a median of {{summary.median_se_ratio:2}} times the unweighted one (interquartile range {{summary.q25_se_ratio:2}} to {{summary.q75_se_ratio:2}}). @fig-se (panel A) shows where this comes from. Weighting alone, with every observation its own cluster, raised the standard error by a median factor of {{summary.median_r_weights:2}}; clustering persons within households added {{summary.median_r_cluster:2}} on top of that, and the replicate-weight formula a further {{summary.median_r_formula:2}} (fifth to ninety-fifth percentile {{summary.q05_r_formula:2}} to {{summary.q95_r_formula:2}}). An unweighted fit whose standard errors were clustered on households differed from its model-based standard errors by a median factor of only {{summary.median_r_unw_cl:2}}. The unweighted analyses were therefore not wrong about the precision of what they estimate, an association among respondents; the large standard errors are the price of estimating the population association with unequal weights.

Under each study's declared inference (unweighted for six studies, weighted with household-clustered errors for one; the study that itself used the jackknife is excluded), {{summary.h3_n_lost:r}} of {{summary.h3_n_sig:r}} coefficients that were significant at the five per cent level were not significant under the design-aware fit, {{summary.h3_share:p0}} per cent with an exact ninety-five per cent interval of {{summary.h3_ci_lo:p0}} to {{summary.h3_ci_hi:p0}} per cent; pooled against the unweighted fit for all studies, the figures are {{summary.n_sig_lost:r}} of {{summary.n_sig_naive:r}}. The share differs by study (@fig-se, panel B; @tbl-census). The point estimates of {{summary.n_sign_flip:r}} coefficients ({{summary.share_sign_flip:p1}} per cent) differ in sign between the unweighted and the weighted fit, but only {{summary.n_flip_sig_naive:r}} of these were significant in the unweighted fit and {{summary.n_flip_sig_both:r}} in both, so most sign changes concern coefficients that are close to zero. The second hypothesis (median ratio above one and a half) and the third (more than one tenth of significant coefficients lose significance, here with a lower interval limit above one tenth) are supported.

![Where the standard-error difference comes from and what it changes. Panel A: ratios of standard errors over all re-estimated coefficients, by source (orange: median). Panel B: share of coefficients, significant under each study's declared inference, that lose significance under the design-aware fit, by study.](figures/fig_se.png){#fig-se}

{{tbl:census}}

A concrete example is the negative binomial study of shared mobility and trips, whose conclusion is that ride-hailing use is a significant predictor of daily trips. The unweighted fit reproduces the printed coefficient ({{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.pct_naive:2}} per cent more trips per additional use in the past month on weekdays) and gives a p-value {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.p_naive:pv}}. The weighted estimate is smaller ({{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.pct:2}} per cent, a change of {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.pct_change:0}} per cent); its household-clustered p-value is {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.p_wrob:pv}} and the replicate-weight standard error of {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.se_design:4}} (against {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.se_naive:4}} unweighted) gives a p-value {{cases.jiao_ride_weekday.p_design:pv}}; on weekends the replicate p-value is {{cases.jiao_ride_weekend.p_design:pv}} (@fig-case, reference letter R). Significance, on which the conclusion rests, therefore depends on both the weighting and the variance estimator. A second example is the effect of being a driver on the count of rides in the zero-inflated model: the estimate changes from {{cases.zhang_driver.b_naive:2}} to {{cases.zhang_driver.b_design:2}}, and the p-value from {{cases.zhang_driver.p_naive:pv}} (unweighted) to {{cases.zhang_driver.p_wrob:pv}} (weighted, clustered) and {{cases.zhang_driver.p_design:pv}} (replicate weights).

![Shared-mobility terms of the weekday (panel A) and weekend (panel B) trip models of Jiao and colleagues, with ninety-five per cent intervals from the unweighted and the design-aware fit. Reference letter R marks the ridesharing row discussed in the text.](figures/fig_case.png){#fig-case}

### Which layer of the design matters

The decomposition in @fig-se (panel A) says that the weights drive the difference and that, on average, the household clustering and the replicate formula add little. This is not a licence to skip the replicate formula. Per study, the median ratio of the replicate-weight to the household-clustered standard error ranged from {{cases.r_formula_min:2}} to {{cases.r_formula_max:2}}, and for individual coefficients from {{summary.q05_r_formula:2}} to {{summary.q95_r_formula:2}} (fifth to ninety-fifth percentile); of the {{summary.n_sig_wrob:r}} coefficients significant under the weighted household-clustered fit, {{summary.n_sig_lost_wrob:r}} ({{summary.share_sig_lost_wrob:p0}} per cent) lost significance under the replicate variance, including the ride-hailing coefficient above. Where replicate weights exist they should be used; the household-clustered weighted fit is a reasonable fallback for the 2022 wave, where the design is expressed through strata and clusters, but it is an approximation that fails in some of exactly the cases that matter.

### Models without a printed coefficient table

The structural equation model of online shopping and shopping trips, which prints standardised coefficients, was fitted with the same variables except two that come from other sources, on {{p02.n:i}} persons against the printed {{design.printed_sem_n:i}}. Its two cross-effects were {{p02.prop_purchase_est.weighted:2}} and {{p02.prop_shoptrp_est.weighted:2}} in our weighted fit against {{p02.prop_purchase_est.pub:2}} and {{p02.prop_shoptrp_est.pub:2}} printed, with design standard errors of about {{p02.prop_purchase_est.se:2}}. One cross-effect has the opposite sign and the other a different size, and the sign convention of the latent variables cannot repair both; we grade the model as not reproduced. For the propensity-score matching study of ride-hailing and vehicle miles, a greedy nearest-neighbour matching in the same strata gave {{p22.triples:i}} matched triples of persons with household vehicle access against about five thousand printed. Matched mean daily miles differed from the printed means (for frequent users {{p22.vmt_frequent:1}} against {{p22.pub_frequent:1}} miles) and only one of the three vehicle contrasts was close to its printed value (non-users to occasional users {{p22.veh_no.naive:3}} against {{p22.veh_no.pub:3}}); we grade the study as not reproduced. A design-aware comparison of matched samples is not straightforward, because weighting the two arms separately breaks the pairing and the replicate variance treats the matched sample as fixed; we report only that none of the three vehicle contrasts has a t statistic above two when the arms are weighted ({{p22.veh_no.t_design:2}}, {{p22.veh_of.t_design:2}} and {{p22.veh_nf.t_design:2}}), without comparing it with the paired statistic of the paper ({{p22.veh_no.t_paired:2}} for the first contrast).

### Machine-learning models

Classifiers of alternative-fuel and electric vehicle adoption showed the largest dependence on the pipeline (@fig-leak). When the rarer class was oversampled before the rows were split, the area under the curve of the random forest was {{ml.afv.leaky.rf:2}} (alternative-fuel vehicles) and {{ml.ev.leaky.rf:2}} (electric vehicles) and of the decision tree {{ml.afv.leaky.dt:2}} and {{ml.ev.leaky.dt:2}}. When the split came first, the same models scored {{ml.afv.rows.rf:2}} and {{ml.ev.rows.rf:2}} for the random forest and {{ml.afv.rows.dt:2}} and {{ml.ev.rows.dt:2}} for the tree; splitting by household changed this little ({{ml.afv.grouped.rf:2}} and {{ml.ev.grouped.rf:2}}), as expected because only {{holdout.share_rows_shared_household:p0}} per cent of the rows share a household with another row, so the leak that matters here is the oversampling. Weighted by the survey weight, the random forest scored {{ml.afv.weighted.rf:2}} and {{ml.ev.weighted.rf:2}}. The inflation of the random forest was {{ml.afv.infl_rf:2}} (alternative-fuel) and {{ml.ev.infl_rf:2}} (electric); the decision tree, which scored {{ml.afv.leaky.dt:2}} in the leaky pipeline, is barely better than chance ({{ml.afv.dt_grouped:2}}) when evaluated honestly.

The printed values for alternative-fuel vehicles, {{ml.pub.rf:2}} for the random forest and {{ml.pub.dt:2}} for the decision tree, lie between the leaky and the honest scores and are reproduced by neither (@fig-leak, reference letter L); our sample is also smaller than the printed one. The printed accuracies, above ninety per cent for all five models, are consistent with an honest test set of a rare class, where predicting the majority class gives {{ml.acc.afv.weighted.rf:2}}, and not with the leaky pipeline, where accuracy was {{ml.acc.afv.leaky.lr:2}} for logistic regression, {{ml.acc.afv.leaky.nb:2}} for naive Bayes and {{ml.acc.afv.leaky.svm:2}} for the support vector machine. We therefore do not claim that the published pipeline leaked; we show that oversampling before splitting inflates the score of three of five models by more than fifteen percentage points (the random forest by {{ml.afv.infl_rf:2}}, the decision tree by {{ml.afv.infl_dt:2}} and the support vector machine by {{ml.afv.infl_svm:2}}) and of the other two, logistic regression and naive Bayes, by {{ml.afv.infl_lr:2}} and {{ml.afv.infl_nb:2}}. The fourth hypothesis, as originally worded (the printed score is reproduced only in a leaky pipeline), is not supported; the inflation it rests on is. Tuning all models alike did not remove the gap. The tuned random forest scored {{ml.tuned.afv.leaky.rf:2}} when oversampling came first and {{ml.tuned.afv.grouped.rf:2}} by household (an inflation of {{ml.tuned_infl_rf_afv:2}}; for electric vehicles {{ml.tuned_infl_rf_ev:2}}), and the tuned decision tree rose from {{ml.afv.dt_grouped:2}} to {{ml.tuned.afv.grouped.dt:2}} but stayed far below its leaky score of {{ml.tuned.afv.leaky.dt:2}}. The largest standard deviation of a mean score over the seeds was {{ml.seed_sd:3}} for the default settings and {{ml.seed_sd_tuned:3}} ({{ml.seed_sd_tuned_w:3}} for the weighted score) for the tuned models.

{{tbl:auc}}

![Area under the ROC curve of five classifiers under four pipelines, for alternative-fuel vehicles (panel A) and electric vehicles (panel B). Filled circles: default settings of the first experiment; open triangles: all models tuned alike. Reference letter L marks the printed random-forest score of the study.](figures/fig_leak.png){#fig-leak}

The regression study of household online shopping printed held-out R-squared values of {{p21.w2017.gbm.pub:2}} for gradient boosting in 2017 and {{p21.w2009.gbm.pub:2}} in 2009. Our boosting model on the public variables that correspond to the printed list reached {{p21.w2017.gbm.random:2}} and {{p21.w2009.gbm.random:2}} on randomly held-out households and {{p21.w2017.gbm.state:2}} when whole states were held out (@fig-r2). The validation design does not explain the gap: even on its training households the model explained only {{p21.w2017.gbm.train:2}} in 2017, and our linear regression scored {{p21.w2017.lr.random:2}} against {{p21.w2017.lr.pub:2}} printed, so the target or the variables differ. The printed variable table contains percentages above one hundred and a variable listed twice, so we cannot say which variables entered the printed model, and we make no claim about its correctness or about leakage.

![Held-out R-squared of four regression models for household online purchases in 2009 (panel A) and 2017 (panel B): printed values and our values for random and for whole-state hold-out.](figures/fig_r2.png){#fig-r2}

## Discussion

**What the ladder says.** For a typical NHTS regression, the printed numbers are recoverable from the public files, provided the reader knows whether the authors weighted, which the paper often has to be read twice to give; where the two estimators can be told apart, the declared one reproduces the printed numbers. The next rung is where the findings move. The design-aware standard error is a median of {{summary.median_se_ratio:1}} times the unweighted one, and under the studies' own declared inference {{summary.h3_share:p0}} per cent of the significant coefficients are not significant under the design. These are not errors in the original papers, most of which state what they did; they show that the choice between an unweighted and a weighted, design-aware analysis has consequences that the articles rarely discuss.

**What the standard errors mean.** The unweighted analyses estimate an association among respondents, and their standard errors are nearly right for that estimand (understated by a median factor of only {{summary.median_r_unw_cl:2}}). The design-aware standard errors are large because estimating the population association with unequal weights is less precise. A planner who wants to project demand needs the population association and therefore the weighted fit with its honest uncertainty; a researcher interested in respondents may legitimately stay unweighted, but should say so. In the ride-hailing example, the coefficient is small under both fits, its significance, on which the headline rests, depends on the estimator, and the weighted estimate is a quarter smaller than the unweighted one. For the vehicle-miles matching study, our matched samples do not reproduce the printed contrasts, so we make no statement about vehicle shedding.

**Why clustering matters little here.** Persons of a household share location, income and vehicles, but the outcomes studied (trip counts, mode use) are only weakly correlated within households once the covariates are in the model, and many rows have no other member in the sample. The effect of weights on the standard error is much larger because the NHTS weights vary strongly across persons. Replicate weights add the stratification and the unequal selection and change individual verdicts, so they should be used when available.

**The prediction scores.** Oversampling before splitting inflates the score of a decision tree, a random forest and a support vector machine by more than fifteen percentage points, a leak documented in other fields [@kapoor2023; @demircioglu2024]. The printed scores are not reproduced by either pipeline and the printed accuracies argue against the leaky one, so the result is a warning, not a verdict on the original studies. A reader can check any pipeline with `pynhts.validate.audit_classifier`, which takes a few seconds. When the data are split before oversampling, a random forest of alternative-fuel adoption has an area under the curve of {{ml.afv.grouped.rf:2}}, about that of logistic regression ({{ml.afv.grouped.lr:2}}), which is modest and worth knowing before using it to target adoption policy. The regression-score gap of the online shopping study is of another kind: the validation design does not explain it.

**Implications for the package.** The study required tools that did not exist in the package: a regression that returns weighted estimates with the wave's variance design, a check of prediction pipelines for leakage, and a way to compare a printed number with a rebuilt one. The first two are released in pynhts as `pynhts.models` (now with the unweighted, clustered, weighted and design-aware fits and a warning when the verdicts differ) and `pynhts.validate`, validated against R for the replicate-weight and the Taylor designs, and the rules of the package's agent guide say to use them. Three further developments follow from the evidence and are planned: a formula interface and ordinal and multinomial families for the discrete-choice papers that the present set does not include; household-level multilevel models with partial pooling for regional comparisons; and a library of replication recipes, one per published study, so that the registered gaps become regression tests that any user can run. The package also ships the Compendium of Uses as `pynhts.compendium`: the {{compendium.n_unique:i}} distinct studies with their editions, chapters and the keyword tags used here, a search and BibTeX export, an audit of how the corpus was parsed, and an advisor that, for a topic such as electric-vehicle adoption or bike sharing, lists what earlier studies did and which of the pitfalls measured in this paper apply. The {{compendium.n_case_in_compendium:r}} audited studies that the Compendium lists are linked to their rung on the ladder, so that any other entry can gain a replication recipe in the same way.

**Limitations.** The case-study set is a convenience set of {{ladder.n_studies:r}} studies, and {{ladder.n_l2_attempted:r}} of them were refitted; the share of fragile conclusions among all NHTS papers is therefore not estimated. The pooled census mixes studies of different size; the declared-inference version restricts the comparison to what each study did. Two zero-inflated studies could not be graded because their printed headline cannot be mapped onto a coefficient; they contribute design effects only. Our fits reproduce some printed values only approximately because the published samples cannot be rebuilt exactly. The matching study used a greedy matching, not the optimal matching of the original. The machine-learning experiments use five classifiers with ten tuning trials each, a modest search that makes the comparison fair but not exhaustive, and score person rows with the household weight. We did not test whether the weights are informative about the outcomes, which would be the formal basis for choosing between the weighted and the unweighted estimand [@bollen2016]. The statements on how the wider literature reports weights and variance rest on our register and on keyword tags of the abstracts of the Compendium, not on a review of full texts: on the positives that we read the tags have a precision of {{compendium.review_weights_precision:p0}} per cent for weights and {{compendium.review_variance_precision:p0}} per cent for variance estimators (recall was not measured), an abstract that does not name the weights may still have used them, and the Compendium is an official list, not the whole literature. The 2022 wave, which has no replicate weights, would use linearisation; it is implemented and checked against R but not exercised on the case studies. Finally, we describe conclusions as design-sensitive; we do not say they are wrong.

**Recommendations.** For authors: name the weight variable (`WTPERFIN` for persons, `WTHHFIN` for households, `WTTRDFIN` for trips), say whether weights were used and why, and for which population the coefficients are meant; report standard errors from the survey design (the replicate weights, or strata and clusters for the 2022 wave) or, when neither is used, with household-clustered errors and a statement that they are an approximation; analyse a subgroup as a domain of the full sample and not by dropping the other rows; and give the sample-flow table with the number of records removed by each rule. For prediction models: split by household before anything else, oversample only the training rows, report a weighted score, and tune every model alike. For reviewers: a significance star from an unweighted NHTS regression is a statement about respondents, and an area under the curve from a random split of oversampled rows should trigger a question.

## Conclusions

A four-rung reproducibility ladder with design-aware re-estimation turns a general worry about survey-based transport research into numbers. On {{ladder.n_studies:r}} published NHTS studies, the printed numbers were recoverable with the declared estimator where the estimators can be told apart; design-aware standard errors were about {{summary.median_se_ratio:1}} times the unweighted ones, almost entirely because of the unequal weights; {{summary.h3_share:p0}} per cent of the coefficients that were significant under the studies' own inference were not significant under the design; and oversampling before splitting inflated the scores of classifiers of vehicle adoption by up to {{ml.afv.infl_dt:2}} area under the curve, while the printed scores were reproduced by neither pipeline. The machinery is released as `pynhts.models` and `pynhts.validate`, so that other researchers can run the same check on their own analyses.

## Supplementary material

**Deviations from the analysis plan** (the full log is in `analysis_plan.md`): three studies were run before the plan was frozen; the grading tolerance had a floor of two units of the last printed digit; hypothesis three was evaluated against each study's declared inference (the first draft pooled against the unweighted fit); hypothesis four was reformulated after the printed score proved reproducible by neither pipeline; the tuned run used two seeds; a decomposition of the standard-error ratio, an unweighted household-clustered fit and a check of Newton against exact replicate refits were added after an external review; the printed targets of two zero-inflated studies were dropped because they cannot be mapped onto coefficients.

**Literature search.** The related work rests on three searches in October 2026: keyword and citation searches of OpenAlex and Crossref on survey weights, replicate variance, reproducibility and leakage (query log in the repository, `lit/search_log.md`); a duplication test of the paper's question against twelve neighbouring papers, which found none that re-estimates published NHTS regressions or classifiers under the survey design; and a ScienceDirect LeapSpace review of how NHTS studies handle design, weights and variance. A fourth source is an audit of an official list, the FHWA/ORNL Compendium of Uses of the NHTS: its twelve PDF editions (2006 to 2023) were parsed page by page, anchored on each edition's table of contents, and merged with the interactive-search export of 2023 to 2025; entries were deduplicated by title, tagged by keyword rules for NHTS waves, model families, weights, variance estimators and validation wording, and the parsed counts were compared with independent counts of each edition (@tbl-compendium-audit). Code, rules, checksums and the reading of the positives are in the repository (`tools/compendium/`, `compendium/`). The OpenAlex and LeapSpace searches located literature; they were not used to count how often weights or variance estimators are named. Every reference cited was resolved in Crossref with its metadata and checked against OpenAlex for retraction (`lit/verify_refs.py`, `lit/verified.csv`); references that could not be resolved, and candidates whose subject did not support the sentence they were proposed for, were left out. This is not a formal systematic review.
